there s definitely a lot to unpack here first off rankings aren't always the most accurate way to measure the quality of education at least in the u s where i currently study people actually view them with a lot of skepticism columbia university an ivy league institution literally got in hot water recently for faking their data to boost their ranking so clearly being in the top is not always synonymous with academic integrity or better education furthermore most of these rankings put a heavy emphasis on research output which is possible here thanks to government funding trump willing and with philippine higher ed facing budget cuts year after year i guess the gap was kind of inevitable but the thing is that research focus doesn t really reflect what undergrad students actually experience that s why a lot of people say rankings only start to matter if you're aiming for grad school that said i do agree that the philippine university system is flawed from the outdated curricula to the toxic culture around grades it really can feel like a grind with no space to actually grow as a person but at the same time i wouldn t romanticize harvard students or ivy league life either what you see on tiktok or from student influencers is just the highlight reel of course they only show the good parts also quality doesn t always mean quantity i m only taking classes a semester here in the u s but it s still intense and fast-paced i have friends in harvard and other top schools and they re struggling too both academically and mentally one thing i really appreciate here though is the mental health support at least in my experience it s been way more accessible i ve been able to get free therapy through my college and it s helped a lot here if i told my adviser i wanted to take more than classes they d lowkey side-eye me the standard load is because they want us to have time for extracurriculars or just breathing room there s a whole philosophy behind balance not just stuffing the schedule with units to prove you're working hard i really hope the ph education system moves toward that i ve heard there have been some talks about reducing coursework which is a start but beyond that i hope the system gives professors better conditions too i e less admin work so they have more time for student consultations and space to actually love teaching again

schedule despite two session cancellations this week court spokesman reginald tongol announced yesterday that the impeachment court has advanced anywhere from to days ahead of its initial calendar drastically shortening a process originally expected to drag on until february or march tongol said house prosecutors could finish presenting their evidence for article ii or ill-gotten wealth and potentially conclude their entire case if they drop article iii or bribery by the end of next week now with the way the impeachment trial is going on our impeachment court s confidence is stronger that this will be finished before senate goes on holiday recess he said in a virtual press briefing so by dec we will have a final verdict he added the accelerated timeline stems from the prosecution panel s decision to drop several witnesses from their original list for article ii which tackles the vice president s alleged unexplained wealth prosecutors have used eight of their allocated days and have four days left to present their remaining witnesses which include representatives from banks insurance firms the bureau of internal revenue and the anti-money laundering council amlc tongol said the prosecution might be done with article ii by thursday or friday next week if they decide not to add more witnesses or testimonies once the prosecution rests they will file a formal offer of documentary exhibits before the defense panel opens its -day presentation of evidence he said the court expects the defense to streamline its witness lineup in a similar manner tongol also ruled out at a glance - peñarrubia integrated school has introduced a specialized curriculum called indigenous knowledge systems and practices iksp which includes a natural dyeing subject aimed at preserving local indigenous knowledge - the curriculum was developed through community research and collaboration involving teachers and local government support and focuses on hands-on learning experiences for students using plant materials for dyeing - future stages of the curriculum will expand to include loom weaving and indigenous embroidery emphasizing the importance of community engagement and the cultural significance of the practices being taught baguio city philippines students at peñarrubia integrated school learn chemistry from leaves culture from thread and indigenous history with their own hands they gather plant materials chop and weigh them extract their color and watch plain fibers take on shades of beige brown and rust this is not an extracurricular activity natural dyeing is now part of senior high school the subject is the first offering under peñarrubia integrated school s specialized indigenous knowledge systems and practices curriculum iksp developed to help document teach and sustain local knowledge that educators feared was slowly fading from everyday use the first batch of grade learners took natural dyeing during the second semester of the - school year sherwin zapatero master teacher iii senior high school coordinator and focal person for specialized subjects in deped abra said the curriculum grew from the initiative of adelaida bogayao education program supervisor and indigenous peoples education focal person of the schools division office of abra many indigenous traditions and practices were steadily fading from everyday life zapatero said explaining why bogayao pushed for iksp to be integrated into the senior high school curriculum the aim he said was to help preserve and pass on this cultural heritage to younger generations peñarrubia integrated school was chosen as the pilot site because it already had an established senior high school program before the lessons reached students however teachers and other personnel first went back to the community four research teams were formed to document natural dye sources traditional dyeing processes weaving patterns and designs and indigenous embroidery the teams included teaching and non-teaching personnel from peñarrubia integrated school and the schools division office of abra zapatero said the research and curriculum development were carried out through trainings workshops and collaborative sessions funded under deped s indigenous peoples education program the findings from these community-based studies became the cornerstone of the curriculum he said teachers then translated the documented knowledge into learning competencies lessons and instructional materials aligned with deped standards according to zapatero the curriculum went through technical review validation and quality assurance before it was approved by the deped cordillera administrative region on january zapatero worked with then school principal pepito trinidad and his fellow senior high school teachers in preparing the documents needed for implementation including the feasibility study strategic plan and implementation framework the teachers also helped translate the research into classroom-ready lessons and materials while zapatero developed the curriculum framework and coordinated the submission and review process the municipal government later joined the effort zapatero said the sangguniang bayan under then mayor jane cecilia and then vice mayor geraldine balbuena authorized a memorandum of agreement between the municipality and deped abra through peñarrubia integrated school under the agreement the municipality committed support for an lgu-funded teacher as well as tools equipment and materials needed for the hands-on electives zapatero said the total commitment amounted to p288 including three years of salary for the designated teacher the support has continued under balbuena now the municipal mayor for a subject built around making things by hand that support matters students cannot learn dyeing weaving and embroidery from lectures alone zapatero underwent specialized training in natural dyeing through the department of science and technology philippine textile research institute in partnership with the university of abra that training allows him to teach both the cultural and scientific sides of the process students learn which plant materials can produce color and how these are prepared they also observe how extraction measurement and treatment affect the final shade in class and during outdoor learning sessions plant materials are sorted cut weighed and processed before being used on fibers finished skeins show the results some come out pale and earthy others turn warmer shades of brown and rust something growing nearby becomes pigment pigment becomes thread thread will eventually become textile the process also gives students a practical way of seeing how indigenous knowledge and science meet they are not only told that certain plants can produce dye they test them compare results and work with the materials themselves the next stage of the curriculum will move from dyeing to textile making loom weaving and indigenous embroidery are scheduled for implementation in the third term of the - school year for grade learners who previously completed natural dyeing in grade this progression allows students to deepen their understanding of indigenous craftsmanship while developing practical skills that contribute to the preservation and continued practice of abra s rich cultural traditions zapatero said students first learn where color comes from then how that color becomes part of something woven or embroidered bringing indigenous knowledge into formal education also comes with responsibility the designs and practices being taught are not simply classroom materials they carry histories meanings and identities rooted in communities the knowledge did not begin in school it came from people who practiced it and passed it on long before it became part of a curriculum that makes continued engagement with the community important as the program grows current school principal maria lorena bisares is overseeing the continued implementation and development of the specialized curriculum for the students in the first batch the lessons are practical they learn which plants can produce color how fibers respond to treatment and how those fibers can eventually become woven or embroidered pieces but they are also learning something harder to measure the knowledge behind those processes came from despite these gains the country's scores remain low compared to oecd averages and a large percentage of students still fall below baseline proficiency levels highlighting ongoing educational challenges - the improvements were not evenly distributed with socioeconomically advantaged students seeing greater gains and concerns remain about the sustainability of these results and the overall learning crisis in the education system after a long wait on september we now have the results of the programme for international student assessment pisa which measures the skills of -year-old students there s good news all around philippine scores have improved in all three subjects tested our reading score rose from in to math from to and science from to all three increases were statistically significant meaning the analysis finds evidence of improvement beyond sampling and measurement uncertainty pisa noted that we were among eight participating education systems that exhibited significant gains in all three subjects great in addition the share of filipino students below baseline proficiency in science or pisa s minimum expected skill level also fell by a significant -percentage points between and all of this is welcome news and our teachers and students deserve recognition what accounts for the improvement on the one hand such a result should be hardly surprising given the intense preparations of the department of education deped president ferdinand marcos jr himself directed deped as early as to improve its pisa ranking in response deped formed a task force pisa whose job was to help teachers and especially students prepare for the computerized tests they provided computers to the hundreds of schools which would potentially be sampled at random by the pisa test administrators and took pains to allow students to practice on pisa-type reviewers so that they re less anxious to take the pisa test in case they are chosen to take it these were so-called familiarization sessions during test day itself deped also made sure to put in place a festive mood in the schools to make the exam less scary for students in deped also rolled out a special science program which involved teachers training their students in pisa-type questions this raised concerns that selected students were being trained for the sake of pisa a phenomenon called teaching to the test meanwhile within the deped hierarchy certain regional offices proferred incentives e g awarding of plaques in special events for pisa participating sdos and schools after the exam was administered the idea was to recognize the efforts and commitment of pisa-participating schools and prospectively incentivize continued improvement in learning outcomes to drive future enhancements in educational performance the singular focus of the public education system on pisa seems to have paid off the improvements are real but that s what you get from intense preparation as with any student determined to ace an exam preparation is key the philippines improvement is especially amazing given the broader trend in rich countries showing a significant deterioration especially in reading and math scores according to the official press release average reading scores fell by points across oecd countries between and equivalent to about one and a half years of learning mathematics scores fell by points equivalent to just over one year of learning among non-oecd pisa participants reading scores fell by points and mathematics scores by eight points over the same period whether this unsettling result is because of worsening digital distractions or greater use of ai we don t quite know yet at least for us we seem to be bucking this global trend for now beyond the headline gains of course there s much more to say about the philippines pisa results beyond the headline-grabbing gains first our reading score of is still quite low compared to the oecd average of in math the comparison is versus and in science versus our ranking in asean also still leaves much to be desired figure while we managed to overtake indonesia in reading and math the differences are not statistically significant cambodia managed to overtake us in science so that in the region we re now last in science vietnam which became an upper-middle income country this year like us is also way ahead of us in terms of math and science while the deped was gleeful to list the countries that now rank below us we cannot treat every country below us as a country we overtook some countries and economies below us in were absent in more troubling the vast majority of filipino students are still below the baseline proficiency level called level figure as much as are below-proficiency in reading in math and in science meanwhile of filipino students or nearly two in three were below baseline proficiency level in all three subjects simultaneously the gains were also unequal between and science scores rose by points among the most socioeconomically advantaged quarter of filipino students versus points among the most disadvantaged quarter the latter increase was not statistically significant while the gap widened by a significant points what worked what didn t naturally deped was in a self-congratulatory mood when the pisa results were announced but higher scores do not by themselves establish which specific deped program worked how much it contributed or which specific official deserves credit better instruction could have contributed alongside greater familiarity with the computer platform and question formats preparation can include actual teaching too which means learning and test preparation are not always separable the score increase alone cannot tell us how much came from each deped s preparation materials warrant scrutiny since we joined pisa resources already included computer-based familiarization and practice materials so these may have helped in the most recent round some people allege that deped handpicked good students and schools but pisa follows a prescribed sampling process and the oecd says philippine data met its quality standards the sample included students in schools nonetheless since deped knew weeks in advance which specific schools would participate it s worth asking did pisa-participating schools receive substantial extra support that comparable schools elsewhere did not till now we don t exactly know what happens after random selection and how much additional resources were poured to sampled schools maybe deped should publish the coverage timing and intensity of its preparations so that researchers can study their contribution establishing which measures helped would also inform whether they should reach more schools pisa s coverage has limits too the philippine sample represented about of the country s -year-old population leaving young people outside its coverage whose learning also deserves attention more research needs to be done a study published in the economics of education review studied vietnam s exceptional pisa performance despite being an emerging economy they found that vietnam s advantage persists even after adjustments for better-off students being overrepresented adolescents outside school being excluded and possible differences in test preparation and effort measured household and school characteristics explain only part of vietnam s exceptional performance and much remains unexplained for the philippines that study suggests that poverty alone need not determine educational outcomes researchers must find out how much of our learning gap persists after accounting for family circumstances and who gets tested and what could explain the remainder lingering learning crisis finally by no means do the new results tell us that we have eradicated our long-standing learning crisis apart from the learning poverty rate that previously shocked the country the second congressional commission on education edcom also reported that proficiency rates plummet from in grade abysmal as it already is to as low as by grade edcom s executive director karol mark yee also lamented recently on social media that the national government s budget documents for are replete with the phrase at least nearly proficient meaning that deped s performance indicators are considered met if students are at least nearly proficient not quite proficient karol argues that this is too low a bar and may serve to mask systemic underperformance on top of this education secretary sonny angara also divulged that for the budget proposed by the executive for the aral program amounted to zero aral involves remedial interventions for students lagging in reading as things stand there s also no budget yet to hire teachers next year worse the philippine center for investigative journalism pcij recently reported that politicians have made schools their milking recent pisa gains but that should not lull us into thinking that the education crisis is now gone deped still needs to establish what caused the improvement and whether the measures behind it can help students across the country especially those who remain below baseline proficiency most importantly the deped must ensure that these gains are persistent and not just one-off rappler com jan carlo jc at a glance - the author enrolled in certificate courses at the development academy of the philippines to gain knowledge in geopolitics international relations and maritime security driven by curiosity and the need for practical application in their work - the author advocates for older individuals to return to education believing that their experience can enrich discussions and challenge assumptions ultimately leading to better decision-making and governance i enrolled in three certificate courses at the development academy of the philippines they covered geopolitics international relations strategic futures oceans the law of the sea and maritime security attending these courses virtually became one of the most stimulating things i did this year i did not go back to school because i needed certificates missed homework or had suddenly developed a fondness for deadlines i was curious i wanted to understand what was happening in the world and why but there was a practical reason too i needed this knowledge for my work i wanted to ask better questions and give better advice about policies that matter people at work now come to me with questions about security not because i am an expert but because i am studying it curiosity is a wonderful thing but one has to be useful too abstract until in our maritime security course retired associate justice antonio carpio showed us historical maps they made me appreciate something deceptively simple geography is neither a blessing nor a curse we cannot push china farther north we cannot move taiwan farther south we cannot wish the south china sea away but geography should not determine a nation s fate a short basketball player cannot suddenly become six-foot-eight but he can learn to run faster pass better play stronger defense see the court differently and use what he has to his advantage countries have to do the same thing then came the law attorney fretti ganchoon senior state counsel at the department of justice gave us a terrific lecture on the oceans unclos united nations convention on the law of the sea and international law these can sound terribly abstract until a marine is struck in the head somebody loses a thumb or fishermen come home injured and their wives wonder whether on the next trip they might become widows attorney isabel cañaveral legal officer of the university of the philippines institute for maritime affairs and law of the sea took us through the maritime zones jurisdictions rights and obligations created by unclos after that an ocean no longer looked like empty blue space to me it had boundaries rights responsibilities and consequences simulating a crisis then florence principe gamboa managing editor of facts made us confront what happens when geography law and politics collide with an actual emergency she put us through a simulation involving the evacuation of filipinos from taiwan suddenly geopolitics became very real who is in charge do we know where our people are how do we move some filipinos out of taiwan if commercial flights stop which taiwanese agencies do we coordinate with how do we communicate with our people and our counterparts on the ground and perhaps the most important question has the evacuation plan actually been tested these are not minor operational details in a crisis they may determine whether a plan works at all a plan on paper is not enough discovering its weak points after the crisis begins is already too late that raised another question what if we could think about crises before they happened that was what the strategic futures and national security course taught by dr oliva domingo of the up national college of public administration and governance asked us to do choices that can change a future strategic foresight is not fortune-telling it is a disciplined way of looking at several plausible futures using what we know today while recognizing what we do not know i chose chronic kidney disease not because i wanted to turn kidneys into a security threat but because disease on a large enough scale affects a country s choices read opinion philippines peculiar health policy waiting until kidneys fail young people on dialysis will not be joining the armed forces or the coast guard and when government spends billions treating preventable disease those resources come from the same national budget that must also fund education infrastructure social protection and security my paper therefore was not really about kidneys it was about choices made early enough to change a future i developed several scenarios in the future i considered most desirable government acted much earlier preventing diabetes and hypertension regulating unhealthy food environments giving incentives to urban and town planners to create places where people could walk play and socialize and teaching children early about eating well and staying healthy by the time a problem becomes a crisis our choices have already narrowed and across all these subjects maps oceans evacuation plans chronic disease one issue kept returning governance security does not exist only at sea at a border or inside a military installation it depends on whether institutions work agencies speak to one another responsibilities are clear and whether somebody has thought about what happens on monday morning after the crisis erupts on sunday night i came away with a conviction that sounds almost embarrassingly ordinary grand strategies do not work unless somebody makes sure the operational details work too what older people bring to the classroom which brings me to the dap learning team led by dean alyn joy baltazar they worked quietly in the background making sure lecturers and students remained connected despite weak and unreliable internet schedules ran on time lectures were recorded transcribed and uploaded promptly submissions met deadlines and spotify somehow managed to play the coolest music during our breaks in class we talked about governance coordination and institutional capacity the dap learning team demonstrated all three without announcing that they were doing so these courses made me question assumptions test the logic of my own arguments discard ideas i had become too comfortable with and look at familiar problems differently i brought experience into the classroom not necessarily wisdom i have worked in policymaking and implementation nationally and internationally i have seen policies succeed and fail i have watched institutions evolve more importantly i have known people whose lives were affected by all of them experience changes the questions one asks i can still be impressed by an idea but i am much more interested now in whether it works who will implement it what happens when it reaches the bureaucracy what happens when conditions change and ultimately how will it make people s lives better that is why i hope more older filipinos return to classrooms we need places where generations can meet where experience encounters new knowledge where assumptions can be challenged and where people can disagree without pretending that anyone already has all the answers i went back to school because i was curious i also wanted to be useful i came away understanding something i had not expected education does not change the map it changes how we read it and that can change what we decide to do next rappler com marilen j danguilan is a medical doctor who studied at the university of the philippines diliman the london school of economics and life as a student can sometimes feel like waking up every day already exhausted the alarm rings before the sun comes up and there s barely enough time to gather the energy to face another day of school books assignments and expectations pile up endlessly making it feel like there is never a moment to truly rest even when surrounded by classmates many students quietly carry their stress alone afraid that no one else really understands the pressure to succeed can weigh heavily on young minds every test every assignment and every grade can feel like a judgment of their worth a single mistake may linger in their thoughts for days making them question whether they are good enough students often compare themselves to others who seem smarter or more confident and that comparison can slowly drain their motivation and self-belief long nights of studying can leave students staring at their desks while the rest of the world sleeps the quiet hours can feel lonely filled with worry about unfinished work or upcoming exams sometimes the effort they put in still doesn t lead to the results they hoped for and that disappointment can make them feel trapped in a cycle of trying harder but still feeling behind friendships which should make school life brighter can also bring pain misunderstandings arguments or feeling left out can turn an ordinary day into a difficult one a crowded hallway may still feel isolating when someone feels like they don t belong anywhere small moments like sitting alone at lunch or being ignored in a group can stay in a student s mind long after the day ends many students also worry about their future long before they feel ready to questions about careers university and expectations from family can feel overwhelming it may seem like every decision they make now could affect the rest of their lives that kind of pressure can make the future look less exciting and more frightening sometimes students hide their struggles behind quiet smiles they show up to class complete their work and act like everything is fine even when they feel drained inside it can be hard to tell others how difficult things feel especially when everyone else seems busy with their own problems the routine of school can start to feel endless wake up study worry sleep and repeat days blur together and it may seem like there is no break from the stress even weekends can disappear under piles of homework and preparation for the next week despite all this many students continue pushing forward because they believe things can eventually improve they keep trying learning from mistakes and slowly building resilience through difficult moments the challenges they face can be incredibly tough but they also shape patience determination and strength over time some students begin to realize that they are not alone in their struggles others around them are also tired worried and trying their best sharing those experiences with friends or trusted adults can make the burden feel a little lighter student life can be deeply challenging but it is also a period of growth the long nights the stress and the doubts may leave scars yet they can also teach valuable lessons about perseverance and empathy even in the hardest moments many students keep moving forward hoping that the future will eventually be brighter

shifts with students each shift crowded into classrooms that can barely fit the or so pupils crammed into them for four hours each day yet just steps away another three-storey school building has stood idle empty and unfinished for nearly two years funded through the basic education facilities fund beff the government s annual school construction budget the p32-million project was contracted to quezon-based l a clamor construction the cavite 3rd district engineering office of the department of public works and highways dpwh said the contractor needed to do extensive structural work it can be completed but the project was put on hold said school head ramon novicio because the request for additional funding was made for a four-storey building when the actual building was only three stories because of that error the project has been stuck in bureaucratic limbo the mabuhay school is emblematic of the problems hobbling the government s school infrastructure program following the flood control scandal last year president marcos canceled the flood-control budget and transferred a big chunk of it to education as much as p80 billion was allocated to the school infrastructure budget but that brings little comfort for the students and faculty of the mabuhay school no matter how intelligent and effective teachers are in delivering instruction some learners will encounter classrooms were unusable in addition classrooms have yet to be built this year s school infrastructure budget is the biggest in eight years in the past poor planning and faulty and fraudulent procurement have derailed the government s school building program can the two government departments education and public works deliver this time and will school infrastructure projects be immune to the anomalies that have long plagued public works pcij analyzed more than school infrastructure contracts awarded by the dpwh from to our findings show that the problems that hounded flood-control projects were evident in school projects as well these include - projects that were awarded to politically well-connected contractors with a history of graft and substandard construction - lobbying by legislators and other officials which influenced what projects were funded favoring some areas despite the need to distribute projects equitably across the country and - bureaucratic red tape and delays in the identification of projects which resulted in huge backlogs in project implementation the government has taken measures to limit fraud and corruption including assigning projects to local governments and dpwh regional rather than district engineering offices which were the hub of corruption in flood-control projects cases have been filed against erring contractors some of whom have lost their licenses and been banned from public works projects still skeptics ask does the government have the administrative capacity to solve the classroom shortage with p400 billion needed to address the backlog can it deliver quality school buildings on time and ensure that taxpayers money is not lost to corruption here are our findings in the past years the discaya and co families reaped billions from school infra contracts most school construction funds are lodged with the deped while the dpwh oversees procurement and implementation data from the dpwh transparency portal reveals that contractors tied to the flood control scandal were the same ones awarded a large share of school infrastructure contracts construction tycoons curlee and sarah discaya bagged some p13 billion worth of davao occidental and bulacan flood control projects nine discaya companies have had their licenses revoked by the philippine contractors accreditation board dpwh records show the couple secured p232 at a glance - edcom i in the early 1990s recognized the educational needs of indigenous learners recommending resources for tribal schools and culturally relevant materials - over the years indigenous communities have led efforts to integrate indigenous knowledge and learning systems into the national education framework emphasizing the importance of cultural integrity and community involvement - recent policies from deped have aimed to strengthen indigenous peoples education by ensuring that education is culturally relevant and developed in partnership with indigenous communities moving beyond mere inclusion to genuine collaboration in the early 1990s the first congressional commission on education or edcom i looked at the needs of what it called special target clientele in recommendations that appear to refer to indigenous learners and communities edcom i was brief provide resources to tribal and mission schools develop indigenous appropriate instructional materials and train teachers to use them this was not insignificant it recognized needs the school system was not meeting but three decades later one sees the limits of that framing indigenous peoples education or iped is not just about bringing schools books teachers and classrooms to far-flung communities it is about deeper questions - what kind of learning enables indigenous children to remain rooted in who they are while gaining competencies to move across different spaces without leaving their identity behind - how should education programs be pursued with indigenous communities in ways that interface with indigenous learning systems rather than simply expecting communities to conform to a state-defined curriculum and education system for years that broader vision was carried mainly by indigenous communities themselves with mission and community-based schools civil society organizations and advocates they opened spaces where the national curriculum could meet indigenous knowledge languages histories values and ways of learning these efforts challenged colonial habits the privileging of school-based and textbook knowledge the treatment of culture as an add-on and the tendency to divide learning neatly into subjects in indigenous contexts learning is often more holistic woven through their ancestral domains work ritual relationships memory and responsibility i had the privilege of learning this directly when during the term of education secretary armin luistro i was tasked to lead the department of education s work in setting up the national iped program a process guided largely by indigenous communities themselves i say learning deliberately because the most important work was not for deped to develop a program for indigenous peoples it was to listen and understand building on previous efforts deped from to pursued a more deliberate relationship with indigenous elders leaders community representatives and iped practitioners during this period deped began putting in place a clearer framework office budget and policies for iped deped order no issued in adopted the national iped policy framework it placed participation inclusion empowerment dialogue and partnership at the center and defined what a national iped program should cover the indigenous peoples education office ipseo gave the program a focal point inside the bureaucracy while iped received an annual budget line item in government commitments have to be translated into structures staff time procedures and funds otherwise even beautiful policy language remains ceremonial also on rappler - time trowel how to truly decolonize the philippines educational system - opinion mother tongue-based education and our indigenous peoples - opinion iksp ay ksp we have to pay attention to indigenous knowledge - what it takes to keep tboli children in school deped order no issued in guided schools to ensure that activities materials and representations involving indigenous culture proceed with proper consent context and respect it responded to a familiar problem cultural expressions were often presented casually or inaccurately without sufficient regard for the communities to whom they belong the policy reminded schools that cultural inclusion cannot mean cultural appropriation deped order no issued in adopted the iped curriculum framework it made clear that iped is not simply inserting indigenous content into existing lessons it is about the interface between indigenous learning systems and the national education system it recognizes elders culture bearers indigenous knowledge holders community history ancestral domain and community life as integral to learning it also makes clear that there can be no single uniform ip curriculum indigenous peoples in the philippines are diverse and indigenizing education has to happen through local dialogue and partnership on how each community s knowledge values aspirations and competencies interface with the national curriculum in deped order no strengthened this direction through consultative and advisory bodies at the regional schools division and school levels in areas implementing iped composed of indigenous community members selected by elders and other representatives these bodies allow communities to shape in a sustained way how iped is implemented monitored improved and assessed of course access also mattered many indigenous communities long lacked nearby schools after do62 was issued in deped intensified initiatives to establish schools for indigenous peoples in geographically isolated and disadvantaged areas by - this culminated in deped s largest single effort to establish schools for indigenous communities in mindanao alone new schools opened in sy - indigenous learners need schools they can reach and schools where their culture identity and community aspirations are celebrated and nurtured it is encouraging that under secretary sonny angara deped has expressed the intention to advance inclusion and remain open to different ways of doing things equally important edcom ii has shown openness and courage in asking difficult questions about the education system as edcom ii and education leadership revisit iped questions on schools teachers classrooms learning materials and support are urgent they should also lead to a deeper one whether education offered to indigenous learners is truly culture-based rights-based and shaped through sustained partnership with their communities the discourse has matured because indigenous communities insisted that education is not neutral when it erases memory weakens identity or treats ancestral knowledge as inferior it matured because policies were not only written for communities but developed with them the task now is to build from the foundations already laid to honor what has been built examine it honestly and deepen it this means measuring progress not only by enrollment numbers or school locations but by standards that communities helped define and deped s foundational iped policies articulate cultural integrity flourishing identity meaningful participation sustained partnership and the continuing interface between indigenous learning systems and the national education system if edcom i opened a small window the work since then shows that the door is much wider the task now is to keep widening that door by continuing the work already begun listening unlearning and working in genuine partnership with indigenous communities indigenous peoples education is not a special project at the margins it is part of making philippine education more inclusive truthful and able to honor the many ways of being filipino rappler com rozanno butch rufino served as adviser to the secretary on indigenous
